extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on performing 35 U.S.C. 101 subject matter eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106), including claim construction (BRI), the Alice/Mayo two-part test, and related procedures for formulating rejections and evaluating responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two criteria for subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories. Second, the claimed invention also must qualify as patent-eligible subject matter, i.e., the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-part framing (statutory category + not directed to a judicial exception unless 'significantly more') is the core of the §101 analysis and references the Alice/Mayo framework. See MPEP §2106.03 and §2106.04 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories (35 U.S.C. 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 defines four categories: processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter. The latter three define 'things' or 'products' while the first defines 'actions' (a series of steps or acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining whether a claim falls in a statutory category, verify the claim is to a process (method/series of acts) or to a physical/tangible machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. See MPEP §2106.03 for authoritative definitions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility. The BRI sets the boundaries of the coverage sought by the claim and will influence whether the claim seeks to cover subject matter that is beyond the four statutory categories or encompasses subject matter that falls within the exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine applicant's invention by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims under BRI (see MPEP §2111). Claim interpretation affects Step 1 and both prongs of the Alice/Mayo test; if BRI covers non-statutory embodiments recommend amendments narrowing the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2 (the Alice/Mayo test) is a two-part test: Step 2A — determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature or a natural phenomenon (a judicial exception). Step 2B — if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility. The second part is described as the 'search for an "inventive concept"'. The machine-or-transformation test may be considered as part of the 'integration' or 'significantly more' determination but is not a separate test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways A, B, and C for eligibility (flowchart)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three pathways to eligibility are identified: Pathway A (claims falling within a statutory category whose eligibility is self-evident — streamlined analysis), Pathway B (claims within a statutory category and not directed to a judicial exception — Step 2A: NO), and Pathway C (claims within a statutory category, directed to a judicial exception, but reciting additional elements that amount to significantly more — Step 2B: YES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim could have been found eligible at Pathway A but is subjected to further analysis, it may still be eligible at B or C. If not eligible at any pathway, the claim is patent ineligible under 35 U.S.C. 101. Examiners uncertain whether to use streamlined analysis are encouraged to conduct a full eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1: Whether a claim is to a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 asks: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter? Evaluation of this step should be made after determining what applicant has invented and construing the claims in accordance with BRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category, it fails Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If the BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1; best practice is to point out BRI and recommend narrowing amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of product claims that are not statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to any statutory category include: products that do not have a physical or tangible form (e.g., information/data per se or a computer program per se claimed as a product without structural recitations); transitory forms of signal transmission (signals per se); and subject matter expressly prohibited from patenting (e.g., humans per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product claims must have physical or tangible form to fall within machine/manufacture/composition categories. Software expressed as code detached from any medium or an intangible collection of information may be non-statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A: Whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena are judicial exceptions and not patent eligible unless the claim integrates the exception into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim 'is directed to' an exception using the court precedents (Alice, Mayo, Diehr, Benson, Flook, Bilski). If directed to an exception, proceed to Step 2B to assess whether additional elements confer 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas — groupings, examples, and tentative abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas encompass concepts such as certain methods of organizing human activity, mathematical formulas, and mental processes. The MPEP provides groupings and examples to help identify when claims do or do not recite abstract ideas, and notes some 'tentative' abstract ideas where further analysis is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the MPEP examples and groupings (2106.04(a)(1)-(3)) to determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea; consider whether claimed steps are merely mental processes or fundamental economic practices, or if they integrate an idea into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature, natural phenomena & products of nature — 'markedly different characteristics' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims implicating laws of nature, natural phenomena, or products of nature, assess whether the claimed subject matter exhibits markedly different characteristics compared to the natural product or phenomenon as found in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a product of nature, examine whether it has been markedly altered or provided with distinctive characteristics by human intervention (see MPEP §2106.04(b)-(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A prong two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed judicial exception is integrated into a practical application — for example, by improving the functioning of a computer or other technology, or by providing particular treatment or prophylaxis — such that the claim is not 'directed to' the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claim elements, when taken as a whole, apply the exception in a practical way (see MPEP §2106.04(d), including 2106.04(d)(1) for computer/tech improvements and 2106.04(d)(2) for particular treatment/prophylaxis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2B: Whether a claim amounts to significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B asks whether additional elements of the claim, individually or in ordered combination, amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (i.e., supply an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether recited additional elements provide an 'inventive concept' rather than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or insignificant extra-solution activity. See MPEP §2106.05 for detailed sub-factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B subfactor: Improvements to computer functioning or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: One indication of 'significantly more' can be that the claim provides an improvement to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim's limitations improve computer or technological functionality (not merely use generic computer components to perform the abstract idea). See MPEP §2106.05(a) and case examples (e.g., Enfish, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B subfactor: Particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of a particular machine can weigh in favor of eligibility if the machine is specific and integral to the claim rather than a generic computer or token recitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between claims that tie the exception to a specific, claimed machine and those that merely recite a conventional computer. See MPEP §2106.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B subfactor: Particular transformation (machine-or-transformation relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular transformation of an article by the claimed process (the 'transformation' prong of the machine-or-transformation test) can support a finding of 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue and should be considered as part of the 'integration' or 'significantly more' determination, but it is not a separate eligibility test. See MPEP §2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B subfactor: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the field, they do not amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether claim limitations are merely generic or conventional steps that add nothing inventive. See MPEP §2106.05(d) and case law indicating routine/conventional elements are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B subfactor: Other meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Other meaningful limitations beyond mere implementation of the exception — e.g., specific non-conventional steps or details that transform how the exception is applied — can contribute to a 'significantly more' finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider limitations that impose meaningful bounds on the claim or provide technical benefits; see MPEP §2106.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B subfactor: Mere instructions to apply an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are effectively 'mere instructions to apply an exception' (e.g., telling a user to apply an abstract idea) do not add 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claim language is insufficient to confer eligibility; examine whether the claim adds technical implementation details beyond instruction-level recitations. See MPEP §2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B subfactor: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor post-solution activity or other insignificant additional steps do not convert a claim to patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify activities that are purely extra-solution (e.g., data gathering, generic post-solution processing) and treat them as insufficient under Step 2B. See MPEP §2106.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B subfactor: Field of use and technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or technological environment does not by itself make the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims cannot be rendered non-abstract merely by reciting a field of use (e.g., 'apply on the Internet') or technological environment; look for substantive technical improvement. See MPEP §2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis — Eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim's eligibility is self-evident (i.e., clearly not directed to an exception or clearly amounts to significantly more), examiners may use a streamlined analysis (Pathway A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When eligibility is self-evident, a streamlined finding of eligibility at Pathway A is appropriate. If uncertain, conduct the full Alice/Mayo analysis to promote consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis — Clear improvement to a technology or computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that shows a clear improvement to a technology or to computer functionality can be eligible via a streamlined analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP §2106.06(b) examples and case law to determine whether the improvement is clear enough to warrant streamlined treatment (e.g., improvements recognized in Enfish, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must properly formulate rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101, using appropriate form paragraphs and clearly articulating the rationale linking claim limitations to the judicial exception and why additional elements do or do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05, 7.05.01) where appropriate, thoroughly explain the basis of the rejection (identify the exception, explain why claim is directed to it, and explain why additional elements are routine or insignificant), evaluate applicant responses, and clarify the record as needed (see MPEP §2106.07).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate applicant's response and clarify the record
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant responds to a §101 rejection, the examiner should evaluate the response and, if necessary, clarify the record with further explanation or require amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the procedures in MPEP §2106.07(b)-(c) for assessing responses, providing clear rationale, and ensuring the record supports the examiner's position or reasons for allowance after amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 101 is a threshold test — consider other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is not the sole tool for determining patentability; 35 U.S.C. 112, 35 U.S.C. 102, and 35 U.S.C. 103 provide additional tools to ensure claims meet the conditions for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim is eligible under §101, it must still meet novelty, nonobviousness, enablement/written description, utility, inventorship, and other requirements. Examiners should complete examinations under 102, 103, 112, and utility/double-patenting considerations as applicable.
